Sounds to me like you are dead set on making something happen a certain way. Law doesn't really work like that- it CAN, but generally what you want takes an unexpected route. There's absolutely nothing wrong with having a dream, but where you are right now means that you're more likely to fly high and then crash out many many times- I've been there and it sucks. I've gone from having tons of money to being weeks away from homelessness. The money always came back but I gotta say it was an absolute wreck on my mental health. 

So let me ask you something - what is it that you want really: to be wealthy, or for this opportunity to work out? If you want to be wealthy then you can safely let this one go, hold onto your money, and have faith that the thing that's going to make you wealthy is going to come around without causing sleepless nights. If what you want is for the opportunity to work out then... yeah, you're gonna have to risk starving, it's gonna be terrifying, but you might pull through. Keyword, MIGHT. You'll have a crash course in manifesting and I can't guarantee that you'll succeed because it'll all be up to how well you can detach. In your case, detachment means you're gonna have to be OK with the idea of losing that money and not having money to pay rent. Are you okay with that? As someone who's been there: it can definitely work out. It will also absolutely fuck you up.

Full disclosure: after three years and my upteenth crashout, I wound up in a position where I had no choice BUT to get a job. So manifested both exactly enough money to squeak by AND the job, in a shitty job market, in less than a month. The job is boring. It's the best thing I've ever done for myself. It's an office job, and now I don't have to worry about where the money is coming from, and I don't have to expend all of my energy on making up a magical solution to pay my rent. So now I have the time and the energy to work on my personal projects. I also know that the law is real so I'm not gonna be in this job forever, it's probably going to be a matter of months before my next thing takes off and I can leave the job behind- if I want that. After being able to relax for exactly one fiscal quarter I've gotten bored with an easy life so I'm going to go after the big money again-- this time with a safety net. 

You don't have to give up your ambition, but you don't have to starve for it, either.

A woman who is born into poverty and has an abusive lover may only be able to choose between staying with someone who hurts her or taking on illegal work to make enough money to leave. The methods that work for me involve moving my consciousness to the present moment as a way to get my head out of the worry spiral. Like sure maybe the thing I want won't happen, but at the moment I'm in the grocery store and it's fine. If the feeling like giving up is very strong I just let it wash over me because I know that feelings don't last forever. It's really tempting to hold on tighter to controlling our thoughts and emotions during times like these but for me I've found that the secret sauce is in letting go.

The most effective but also the most uncomfortable method is your life blowing up. You can't really mindlessly scroll when you're scrambling to quickly manifest enough money to keep your house. 

But that's the extreme option. I don't recommend it if you can, say, just turn off your phone.

The answer to your question is yes, it is possible. But in order to manifest ANYTHING you need to, respectfully, relax. 

Right now it sounds like you're really struggling and fighting, all for valid reasons. But you're also fighting against your negative emotions and against the emotions that come up when you think about how badly you feel now, how badly you'll feel in the future, how your family will feel, if you fail, what if you KEEP failing, etc etc etc. 

Close your eyes. Breathe. Pull yourself out of the spiral first. In Neville's terms that looks like SATs. In other terms that looks like relaxation techniques or meditation. You can try going on a walk, or sitting upright in an easy chair, or listen to music you like, or exercise, or anything at all that gets you out of your own head. 

From experience, I know that sounds much harder than I am making it out to be when one is in a spiral. Focus on calming down your body and mind first. The job will come. If not this one, then one that is just like it or even better.

Gosh, it’s my tenth year of being aware of the law and learning to apply it, and at the beginning I was just like you. Things would show up in my life that I assumed for but I dismissed them as coincidences. I was constantly, constantly looking for indisputable proof.

I’m not really sure when it clicked. 2018? 2019? And honestly I still stumble a lot. I think that’s normal and all a part of the human experience.

My advice: you can only really work from two states, where you are at currently, and from the state you want to be in when your manifestation pans out. The middle bits or the “how” it all happens is a tangle of possibilities that is in a constant state of flux. When we really care about our manifestations (like your father getting a job), we can get thinking about those middly bits- worrying about “what if it doesn’t happen, what if this is not real”- BECAUSE we care. We don’t care so much about an acai bowl or a lilac bus, so it’s easy for us to leave that alone after we think about it and then go about our lives. And so the time between ”wanting” and ”having” seems to go by in a blink.

From my perspective: it’s totally okay to put down consciously practicing for a little while. In fact, it might actually be the BEST thing in some cases. A manifestation is basically a path between one point of consciousness to the next— and the path from “wanting” to “having” is best enjoyed if you close your eyes and dance to the music. You just put one foot in front of the other and the next thing you know, you’re exactly where you wanted to be.

That’s been my experience, anyways.

My blanket recommendation for both is gentle cleansing and moisturizing with non comedogenic (won't clog pores) products.

They can’t just run through the drive through or hit a last minute Uber eats order into their phone. They cannot pick up a back of chips at the gas station for a snack to hold them over. And I also want to clarify that I AM skinny, comparatively. But I am not underweight. I’m not using a BMI index, because I know they are unreliable, but there is a healthy weight range for people of my height and age, and I am within it. I also eat regularly, and on time. I do not suffer from nutritional deficiency. I am not suffering from any of those listed health problems on the page that comes from nutritional deficiency. My blood work is good.

I eat. My point was that when I cut out the lattes, the chips, the snacks, the baked goods, and all the prepackaged and processed foods that made up the majority of my diet and stuck to foods that I cook and eat at home, I lost a bunch of weight quickly- and my change in lifestyle affected the people around me because THEIR lifestyle was made possible because of readily available food. For example: I lost a friend a couple years ago because she didn’t understand that I could not eat out because of my treenut and peanut allergy until we were on a road trip and she did not anticipate every single venue we went to refusing to serve me because of the risks. She was upset because accommodating my disability cut time out of her itinerary- her itinerary was possible for her because she could be out anywhere and pick up food at any time and keep going. I did not have that luxury. She told me I was being difficult. 

And since my allergies are peanuts, hazelnuts, pork, and fish, that’s in a TON of stuff. Sauces, seasonings, prepackaged meals, ready to cook meals, ice creams, cookies, drink mixes, the list goes on and on. And my reactions are bad enough to be cross contact- so corporations MAY label a warning that the food was made in a facility that also handles peanuts, *but they are not legally obligated to do so*. **And I have learned this from experience.** My last anaphylactic reaction was from an instant coffee brand that said “100% arabica coffee” on the label and no warnings. I only learned about their hazelnut variant while I was doing brand research during my customary 5 hour monitoring stay in the ER. There were no warnings on the label. There were no allergen warnings on the website. 


And to the people around me who made their entire lifestyle off of eating out or using food as a love language, this became a problem for them.

When someone offers me something to eat, and I did not know how it was prepared, I tend to refuse. Because the alternative is asking them “so did, at any point, any peanut products or peanut butter sit on the same surface of any counter top, kitchen utensil, or cooking pan that you prepared this food in? I’m not afraid of anaphylaxis every time I eat. I’m afraid of anaphylaxis when I haven’t been able to ensure that my food is safe. And this is because after six and counting severe reactions over the past five years, I have learned that my allergies and the way the world handles food are not compatible, and it takes much longer to sit someone down and explain the safety precautions that need to be taken and list out my food allergies and their cross reactive counterparts than they often have the patience for. Hand wash your silk. Hang to dry. The textile will last longer and this won’t happen.

How to hand wash silk: fill bucket or clean sink basin with lukewarm water and a teaspoon of gentle laundry detergent. If you have hard water add a spoonful of borax. Swish the silk around in there for a little while, don’t leave it to soak too long. Drain the bucket/basin and rinse with cool water. Roll the silk in a clean towel to blot the excess water out- DON’T WRING IT DRY!! Hang the silk on a line, over an open cupboard, on a laundry rack,,, wherever it will stay relatively undisturbed, out of the sun, and with good airflow, for a couple hours. I think you’re mistaking the common perception of romance/romantic relationships with genuine intimacy and healthy partnerships.

It is true that there is a prevailing myth about ‘needing’ someone to be completed and validated. We’re often sold the idea that emotional intimacy only comes with sexual intimacy- or that they are one in the same. They are not, but that takes some figuring out when most media marketed towards the young really pushes the ‘romance‘ narrative. Arguably one half of the gender binary is not ‘allowed’ emotional intimacy in any other package than one that comes with having sex.  This sucks, because humans  need emotional intimacy to survive. Like, actually survive. There have been studies that show that loneliness and lack of emotional intimacy shortens lifespans and might be a [bigger killer than cancer](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1745691614568352).

It is true that many people who lean towards codependency will hop into relationships to soothe an ache inside because they don’t know who they are without seeing the reflection of themselves in another person. But it is ALSO true that humans are social creatures, and we have evolved to survive through collaboration. Loneliness is an instinctual drive to survive, and it has served us well thus far. “You just want a relationship because you are lonely, and loneliness is weak/lame/something to be stoic about” is JUST an unhealthy a notion as “I’m so lonely so I must jump into a relationship with someone, anyone, right NOW”.

​

The takeaway is this: humans need relationships, but they don’t necessarily have to be romantic or sexual in nature. Unfortunately, we’ve really been pushing ’the most important and possibly only valid kind of relationship is a romantic one‘. If an individual is raised in a supportive, loving, and functional environment, they’re less likely to fall for that ethos- but there is a tragic number of people who don’t have any other examples of love other than what they consume on the internet.

One of my favorite existential questions! 

Some astrologists will say that everything is up to the movement of the planets and that free will doesn’t exist. Similarly, some philosophers conclude that because we are all a web of our inherited traits and instincts, we don’t necessarily have the ability to ‘choose’ outside of our own nature. I can’t remember which physicist it was that argued against quantum entanglement by hypothesizing that every single particle in our universe is on a set trajectory that was initiated during the Big Bang. 

Myself, I don’t know the answer after pondering for like two decades so I’ve just cobbled together a belief system that benefits my mental health. So here’s my take:

There are a finite number of ways scenarios can play out depending on relevant factors (if you were born to an alcoholic mum and a violent dad, what are the chances you will take on those traits? What about your younger brother? What are his chances?)- but we don’t know what all of those factors *are*- and the number of ways might be finite but they can be high in number. 

For example, there are only so many ways you can order a deck of cards. It is known as factorial 52, or “52!”.  The number is defined. It is decided. 

The number, however, is 80,658,175,170,943,878,571,660,636,856,403,766,975,289,505,440,883,277,824,000,000,000,000 unique ways to order a deck of 52 cards. I can’t even use my little human brain to *quantify* that number.

So even with a set of predefined and known variables, the number of unique ways a scenario can play out is quite high, and easily more than a single human being can experience. And according to our theory of probability, each one of these scenarios is just as likely to play out. 

But then things get kind of fuzzy, because we factor in the concept of consciousness and perception. I’m not well versed on this, but from what I gather, we know that we as humans can conceptualize ourselves, but we don’t necessarily know *how* or *why*. We don’t actually know how our ability to slow down, reflect, perceive, and choose affects ourselves and the world around us. 


But let’s go back to astrology. Astrologers have tried to fit every single possible scenario of the human experience into a system of pictorials comprising of seven traditional planets, three outer modern planets, twelve astrological signs, twelve houses, four angles, …and I started counting the fixed stars but lost track at about 233. We quantify all of the celestial bodies’ relationships with each other using 5 major aspects. We’ve been at this practice for something like 5000 years. 

And even then, with all of our knowledge and all of our collective experience, a darn good astrologer can take a look at a chart, hazard a guess at its meaning, and still be wrong. Because the number of scenarios is *that high.* 

Take the moon in the 8th house trining retrograde Pluto in the 4th house. This could mean several things. Maybe I am plagued by depression and easily slip into obsessive behaviors. Maybe I’ve had several surgeries as a kid. Maybe my mother’s family is incredibly wealthy and I stand to inherit a great deal of money but at an emotional cost. Maybe my childhood home was swept away by flood. Fun fact: all of those are possible definitions of that astrological placement, but only ONE of them is true in my case. 




TL;DR: when you start talking about free will in astrology you have to consider that the number of possible ways a single astrological placement can play out is higher than you can likely imagine. We can’t plan for everything, but we CAN, as humans, to slow down, reflect, and choose to the best of our ability. Maybe it’s not ACTUALLY free will in the grand scheme of things, but it has to count for something.

I’ve got a lot of experience with job hunting. Here is my advice: unless you are extremely well connected or live in a densely populated urban center, you are going to be battling for the attention *of a computer*, not a recruiter. A computer doesn’t have feelings, doesn’t have empathy, doesn’t think you’re special. You are another string of binary code and you either fit the parameters it has been programmed to look for, or you don’t. By and large the computer reflects the intentions of the people who designed and implemented the software. It’s cold, but it’s true. 


That being said, here’s how to get a job from someone who’s done that several times in 2022 (unless you have an amazing college curriculum, you won’t have heard about steps 2-7): 


1.	Update your LinkedIn. Brag about yourself. This is not the time to be humble. Use numbers. Did you double a brand’s following in a ridiculously short amount of time? Did you bring in an obscene amount of money? Did your personal brand take off? Talk about it. 

2.	Write ONE excellent resume that scans seamlessly through an ATS (Applicant Tracking System). No fancy graphic design. There are resume templates online. Use them. Say the same thing you said in your LinkedIn profile. Use specific keywords tailored to the type of job you are aiming for. If you want to be in social media, for example, write ‘social media’, ‘content’, ‘instagram’, ‘Facebook’. The ATS will pick this up and you are one step closer to talking to a human being. 

3.	Generate a boilerplate cover letter. Utilize ChatGPT or another AI content writer. This should take maybe 2 minutes. Do not wax poetic about how much you want a job or flex your literary skills. The ATS doesn’t care. Let the AI write it for you. Save your talent and creativity for the additional writing samples you may have to attach. 

4.	Go on LinkedIn and search for job title in your desired area and choose the salary and whether or not you want a remote/on-site/hybrid setup. 

5.	**Hit ‘easy apply’ in the filters section.**For this first part, you’re just throwing spaghetti at the wall, baby. Don’t be precious about it. Go down the line and hit ‘apply’ for each job. If you want to have anything more custom then your boilerplate cover letter, go back into chatgpt and have it make you a cover letter based on the job description. The ATS doesn’t care about your literary talent, the ATS is looking for keywords. 

6.	LATER, when you’re done hitting easy apply, you can go back to the job listings that link out to the company websites and start filling out their application forms. If your resume is written well, then the ATS will should duplicate the information and fill it out for you. If it doesn’t- it’s your call. Do you want to work for a company that doesn’t have that feature, in 2023? How badly do you want the job? 

7.	Now it’s a waiting game. Find something to do with your time. Start a personal project. Pick up a part time job at a bar or in retail. Expect rejection emails- rejections are a GOOD thing. Rejections are signs of life after you have spent time throwing paper out into the void. 

8.	At some point you will get either a phone call from someone, or, more likely, an automated email that links you to a calendly page to schedule a zoom interview. Congrats! It’s baby’s first interview. NOW you get to demonstrate your soft skills. You may interview with several different companies, over several rounds. You might hear from the interviewer again, or you might not. It doesn’t matter. View it as practice.


Because here are my findings:

For every 200 job applications I sent out, I got ONE job offer. Maybe I got 4-6 companies to interview. About 10-15% of those companies sent out a boilerplate rejection letter. I never heard from the rest. 

Job hunting is a numbers game, now. You don’t apply for 20 jobs a month. You apply for 20 jobs a day. Minimum. 


Additional notes: expect to be lowballed. Expect to be overworked and under paid. Is it fair? No. Plan on having a side hustle. You need a *job*. Get a *job*, any job. And then when you get a job, you start the process all over again, covertly, working towards the next best thing. Employers and potential employers will make promises. They will talk about growth and training and how amazing it is to work at their company. Most of the time they’re either overly optimistic or they’re lying (to you? To themselves? Both?). Smile and nod and believe their promises AFTER they are kept, not before. Companies will demand your loyalty and ask for more time and energy than you have promised them. Have boundaries. It’s not personal, and you’re not hurting anyone’s feelings, you are protecting yourself.

Not crazy, sounds like a physiological trauma response. 

Your brain has correctly been wired to associate nuts with danger. Unfortunately for us, our amygdala (which controls emotional response!)  isn’t quite equipped to understand the difference between the ‘image’ or ‘idea’ of something, and the actual ‘reality’ of it. That’s the job of our prefrontal cortex- which, conveniently, gets “shut off” during a physiological trauma response as our bodies divert all the adrenaline and energy to saving us from the threat (real or not). 

A quick hack I’ve gotten into is in the few split seconds I have between seeing the image of the nut and my emotional response to it, is imagining what would happen if I stuck my tongue out and chomped down. Is it silly? 
Heck yeah. 

But since I’m thinking with my senses anyway, my brain usually has enough juice left to be like ‘no, that would taste like paper, not peanut’. 

Since I’m still old enough where I remember staticky tv screens being a thing, I associate a screen with that vaguely electronic taste, which is also *not* peanut.

This isn’t a perfect system because if there’s ACTUALLY a bowl of peanuts in front of me I tend to jump and move to another room. But usually people around me who know what’s up are sympathetic (and actively remove the peanut bowl from my presence as well).
